o: We grow nums1 (length n) by exactly one element to match nums2 (length n+1). The first n positions keep their identity, so position i must travel from nums1[i] to nums2[i] at a cost of |nums1[i] - nums2[i]| unit operations, plus exactly one append. The appended element is a snapshot of some nums1[j]; if taken before index j is modified it equals nums1[j], and afterwards it equals nums2[j]. Hence the extra cost of the copy is min over j of min(|nums1[j] - nums2[n]|, |nums2[j] - nums2[n]|). Checking the examples: [2,8]->[1,7,3] gives 2+1+1=4; [1,3,6]->[2,4,5,3] gives 3+1+0=4; [2]->[3,4] gives 1+1+1=3, all matching.
k: Index i of nums1 can only end at index i, so the positional cost sum(|nums1[i]-nums2[i]|) is unavoidable.
Exactly one append is needed; its source value is either an original nums1[j] (append early) or a finished nums2[j] (append late).

a.i: Sum the mandatory positional deltas, add 1 for the append, and add the cheapest possible snapshot mismatch for the copied element, considering both append-before-modify and append-after-modify sources.
s: Compute base = sum |nums1[i] - nums2[i]| for i < n.
Let t = nums2[n]. Scan j computing min(|nums1[j] - t|, |nums2[j] - t|).
a.t: O(n) - one pass computes the positional sum and the cheapest snapshot simultaneously

w: This is a pure reasoning problem: the whole difficulty is proving the append can be charged min(|nums1[j]-t|, |nums2[j]-t|) for the best j. Pitfall: assuming the appended copy must be an unmodified value only, or that elements can be reordered (they cannot - no deletions or swaps exist). Follow-up: what if nums2 were longer by m elements, or if a 'delete last' operation were added?
